methods.label: Count the arcs for three visible sides
methods.explanation:
Interpret the random point as uniform along the circle, with ordinary unobstructed visibility of an opaque hexagon. The line containing a side determines where that entire side is visible: the observer must lie across the line from the hexagon's center. From this half-plane, sight segments reach every point of the side without crossing the hexagon. From the center's half-plane, sight to an interior point of the side passes through the hexagon first. Positions exactly on an extended side line form a finite set and do not affect the probability.

Let \(O\) be the common center. Joining \(O\) to the vertices divides the regular hexagon into six equilateral triangles of side \(2\). Its circumradius is therefore \(2\), and its apothem, the perpendicular distance from \(O\) to a side, is
\[
a=\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt{3}.
\]
Draw the six rays from \(O\) through the side midpoints. These outward rays are spaced \(60^\circ\) apart.

Each extended side line cuts the surrounding circle at the endpoints of that side's visibility arc. Let \(\beta\) be half the central angle of this arc. The right triangle formed by \(O\), the side midpoint, and an arc endpoint gives
\[
\cos\beta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{r}.
\]
Because the circle surrounds the hexagon, \(r\ge2\), so \(30^\circ\le\beta<90^\circ\). A side is visible precisely when the observer's direction is within \(\beta\) of its outward ray, apart from boundary positions.

Thus all visible outward rays lie in an angular interval of width \(2\beta<180^\circ\). Four rays cannot fit, because four consecutive rays span \(180^\circ\). Three visible rays must be consecutive and span \(120^\circ\). Consequently, if \(\beta\le60^\circ\), seeing three sides has probability zero. The given positive probability therefore requires \(60^\circ<\beta<90^\circ\).

Fix three consecutive outward rays, and let \(t\) be the observer's signed angular displacement from the middle ray. To be within \(\beta\) of both outer rays, the observer must satisfy
\[
60^\circ-\beta<t<\beta-60^\circ.
\]
These bounds also ensure visibility of the middle side. This triple therefore contributes an arc with central angle \(2\beta-120^\circ\). There are six possible triples. Their arcs are disjoint because their centers are \(60^\circ\) apart and each arc has angular width less than \(60^\circ\). Every position seeing three sides belongs to exactly one of them.

Arc length is proportional to central angle on the same circle, so
\[
\frac{6(2\beta-120^\circ)}{360^\circ}=\frac12.
\]
Solving gives \(\beta=75^\circ\). To evaluate its cosine, use complementary acute angles and the sine-difference formula:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\cos75^\circ&=\sin15^\circ\\
&=\sin(60^\circ-45^\circ)\\
&=\sin60^\circ\cos45^\circ
-\cos60^\circ\sin45^\circ\\
&=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This value is positive, so division is valid. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
r&=\frac{4\sqrt3}{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}\\
&=\frac{4\sqrt3(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)}{6-2}\\
&=\boxed{3\sqrt2+\sqrt6}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This radius exceeds \(2\) and gives the required probability. The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

review.mathematicalCheck: The visibility half-plane criterion is justified. The apothem is sqrt(3), so cos(beta)=sqrt(3)/r. Since beta<90 degrees, at most three sides are visible. For beta>60 degrees, the favorable set consists of six disjoint arcs, each of angle 2beta-120 degrees; smaller beta gives probability zero. Thus 6(2beta-120)/360=1/2 gives beta=75 degrees and uniquely r=3sqrt(2)+sqrt(6). The trigonometric evaluation and rationalization are correct, and boundary positions have probability zero.
